title: Left Side Pain After Drinking: Causes and When to Worry
excerpt: Pain in your left side after drinking? What upper left, under-rib, lower left, back, and chest pain usually mean, how to spot pancreatitis, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Pain in your left side after drinking? The common causes, how to spot pancreatitis and other warning signs, what helps at home, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most left-side pain after a night of drinking comes from your gut, not from a serious organ problem. Trapped gas in the bend of your colon, an irritated stomach lining, constipation or diarrhea, and dehydration-related aches are the usual causes, and they fade within a day or two with water, bland food, and rest. The one cause you should never ignore is **pancreatitis**, an inflammation of the pancreas that alcohol is well known to trigger. It usually shows up as a severe, steady pain in the upper middle or upper left of your belly that bores straight through to your back, often with vomiting. That pain is not a hangover, and it needs a doctor the same day. This guide walks through what each kind of left-side pain feels like, where it sits, what you can do at home, and which signs mean you should get checked.

**The quick rules:** Mild, crampy, shifting pain that eases when you pass gas or have a bowel movement is almost always your digestive tract. Severe, constant pain in the upper belly that spreads to your back, gets worse after eating, and comes with vomiting points to pancreatitis. Pain high on the left side of your back, just under the ribs, with fever or pain when you pee points to your kidney. Chest pain on the left, especially with shortness of breath, sweating, or a racing or uneven heartbeat, is a heart warning sign until proven otherwise. Skip alcohol until the pain is fully gone, and go easy on ibuprofen and aspirin while your stomach is irritated.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice, and it can't diagnose you. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if you have** severe upper belly pain that spreads to your back and doesn't let up, pain with repeated vomiting so you can't keep water down, vomit that looks bloody or like coffee grounds, black or tarry stools, chest pain or pressure (especially with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain spreading to your arm or jaw), fainting, a fast or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, a rigid or swollen belly, or confusion. **See a doctor the same day if** you have left-side belly pain with a fever, sharp one-sided pain in your flank that comes in waves, blood in your urine, or pain that's steadily getting worse instead of better. **Book a regular appointment if** you get the same pain every time you drink, even after one or two drinks, or it lasts more than a couple of days. If you could be pregnant, any new one-sided lower belly pain needs prompt care.

## What's on Your Left Side? A Quick Map

It helps to know what actually sits on the left side of your body, because the location of the pain is the best clue you have.

- **Upper left belly, under the ribs:** most of your stomach, the tail of your pancreas, your spleen, and the bend where your colon turns downward (doctors call it the splenic flexure, and it's a classic spot for trapped gas).
- **Upper middle belly, just below the breastbone:** the rest of your stomach and the body of your pancreas. Pancreatitis pain often starts here and spreads left and into the back.
- **Left side of your back, just under the ribs:** your left kidney.
- **Lower left belly:** the last stretch of your colon (the descending and sigmoid colon), where constipation, gas, and diverticulitis tend to cause pain. In women, the left ovary and fallopian tube are here too.
- **Left chest:** your heart, the lining of the lungs, and the muscles and joints of the rib cage.

One useful thing to notice: your **liver is on the right side**, under the right ribs. If you're worried about your liver, right-side pain is the more relevant signal, and we cover it in our guide to [liver pain after drinking](/never-hungover/liver-pain-after-drinking). Left-side pain is usually about the stomach, the colon, the pancreas, or the kidney.

## Pain in the Upper Left Side After Drinking

Upper left abdominal pain, under or just below the left ribs, is the most common version of this complaint. Here are the likely causes, from most to least common.

### Trapped gas in the colon

The colon makes a sharp bend high on the left side, tucked up near the spleen. Gas collects there easily, and it can cause a surprisingly sharp, stabbing pain under the left ribs that sometimes spreads into the left chest or shoulder. Beer, sparkling wine, and sugary mixers add carbonation and fermentable sugars, and alcohol itself changes how quickly food moves through your gut, so bloating and gas are common the next day.

Gas pain tends to move around, comes in waves, and gets better when you burp, pass gas, walk around, or have a bowel movement. Pressing on the area may feel uncomfortable but not exquisitely tender. If this sounds like you, our guide to [gas after drinking](/never-hungover/gas-after-drinking) covers what helps.

### Gastritis (an irritated stomach lining)

Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach directly and increases acid production. After a heavy night, many people get a burning or gnawing ache in the upper middle or upper left belly, often with nausea, a sour taste, burping, or a feeling of fullness after only a few bites. This is acute gastritis. It usually settles within a day or two once you stop drinking, eat bland food, and give your stomach a break.

Gastritis pain often eases a little when you eat something bland and gets worse with coffee, spicy food, more alcohol, or anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin. Those painkillers carry a label warning about stomach bleeding for people who drink, and taking them on an already irritated stomach is a common way to make things worse. Our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) goes deeper on stomach-related causes.

### Acid reflux and heartburn

Alcohol relaxes the valve between your stomach and esophagus, so acid can splash upward. That usually feels like burning behind the breastbone, but some people feel it high in the upper left belly or lower left chest. It's often worse lying down and better sitting up. An antacid usually brings quick relief, which is itself a useful clue.

### Pancreatitis (the one not to miss)

The pancreas sits deep in your upper belly, behind the stomach, with its tail reaching toward the left side near the spleen. It makes digestive enzymes and insulin. Alcohol is one of the two most common causes of acute pancreatitis, alongside gallstones, according to major gastroenterology guidelines and the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK).

The classic picture is:

- **Severe, steady pain** in the upper middle or upper left belly, not crampy or shifting
- **Pain that bores through to the back**, sometimes described as a band around the upper abdomen
- **Nausea and repeated vomiting** that doesn't relieve the pain
- **Pain that's worse after eating** and sometimes eased a little by sitting up and leaning forward
- **A tender, sometimes swollen belly**, often with a fast pulse or fever

It often starts within a day or so of a heavy bout of drinking. Most alcohol-related pancreatitis happens in people who have been drinking heavily for years, but a first attack can come on after a binge, and some people are more susceptible than others for reasons that aren't fully understood. Smoking adds to the risk.

Doctors diagnose it with a blood test for pancreatic enzymes (usually lipase) and sometimes imaging. There's no home treatment. Most cases are mild and improve within about a week in the hospital with IV fluids, pain control, and rest for the gut, but severe cases can be life-threatening. **If your pain matches the description above, go to urgent care or the emergency room. Don't wait it out at home and don't treat it as a bad hangover.**

After a first attack, doctors generally advise stopping alcohol completely, because continuing to drink raises the chance of repeat attacks and, over time, chronic pancreatitis.

### The spleen

The spleen sits under the left ribs. It rarely causes pain from drinking alone. The main time it matters is when it's already enlarged, for example during or after mononucleosis (mono) or in some blood and liver conditions. An enlarged spleen can rupture with a hard knock, such as a fall or a collision, which is more likely after drinking. A sudden, severe upper left pain after a fall or blow, especially with pain at the tip of the left shoulder, lightheadedness, or fainting, is an emergency.

## Left Side Pain Under the Ribs After Drinking

Pain right under the left rib cage is mostly a more specific version of the section above, and the list of suspects is the same: trapped gas at the colon bend, an irritated stomach, and, less often, pancreatitis or the spleen.

Two less dramatic causes are worth knowing too:

- **Muscle and rib cage strain.** Vomiting is hard physical work. Repeated retching can strain the muscles between the ribs and the diaphragm, leaving a sore, achy feeling under the ribs that's worse when you twist, cough, take a deep breath, or press on a specific spot. This kind of pain is usually easy to point to with one finger, and it improves over a few days.
- **Rib cartilage inflammation (costochondritis).** This causes sharp, localized tenderness where the ribs join the breastbone. It isn't caused by alcohol, but a night of coughing, vomiting, or awkward sleeping can bring it out.

A quick self-check: if pressing on one spot on your ribs reproduces the exact pain, and it hurts more when you move or breathe deeply, a muscle or rib cause is likely. If the pain is deep inside, steady, and doesn't change when you press or move, it's more likely coming from an organ, and that's more worth getting checked if it's severe.

## Lower Left Abdominal Pain After Drinking

Pain in the lower left belly usually comes from the last part of the colon.

- **Constipation.** Alcohol can dehydrate you, and dehydration hardens stool. Some people go the other way and get diarrhea, but if you haven't had a proper bowel movement in a couple of days, a dull, crampy lower left ache is a common result. Water, fiber, and gentle movement usually sort it out.
- **Diarrhea and cramping.** Alcohol speeds up the gut and irritates its lining, which can cause cramping on the left side along with loose stools. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains why it happens and what to eat.
- **Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).** If you have IBS, alcohol is a common trigger for flare-ups of cramping, bloating, and changes in bowel habits, and the lower left side is a typical spot for that pain.
- **Diverticulitis.** Small pouches in the colon wall (diverticula) become more common with age, and they sit most often in the lower left colon in Western countries. If one becomes inflamed or infected, it causes persistent lower left pain, often with fever, nausea, and a change in bowel habits. Alcohol isn't a well-established direct cause, but the timing can line up with a weekend of drinking and rich food. Steady lower left pain with fever needs a doctor.
- **For women: ovaries and pregnancy.** An ovarian cyst, ovulation pain, or, importantly, an ectopic pregnancy can cause one-sided lower belly pain. An ectopic pregnancy is an emergency. If there's any chance you could be pregnant and you have new one-sided lower belly pain, especially with spotting, dizziness, or shoulder tip pain, get seen promptly.

## Left Side Back Pain After Drinking

Pain in the left side of the back, high up just under the ribs, is often your left kidney, though the back muscles and pancreas can cause pain there too.

- **Dehydration.** A mild, dull ache in the flank (the area on your side between your ribs and hip) the morning after drinking often reflects dehydration and tends to improve with fluids and rest. It's usually on both sides, not just the left.
- **Kidney stones.** Alcohol doesn't directly cause kidney stones, but dehydration concentrates your urine and can be the trigger that sets a stone moving. A stone causes severe, sharp pain on one side that comes in waves and often spreads toward the groin, sometimes with blood in the urine. Our guide to [whether alcohol causes kidney stones](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-cause-kidney-stones) covers this.
- **Kidney infection.** Flank pain with fever, chills, and burning or frequent urination suggests a kidney infection and needs same-day medical care.
- **Pancreatitis.** As mentioned above, pancreatitis pain often spreads straight through to the back, sometimes more on the left.
- **Muscle strain.** Sleeping in an odd position, a long night on your feet, or vomiting can leave the back muscles sore. Muscle pain is usually worse with movement and better with rest and heat.

For a fuller comparison of kidney pain versus muscle pain, see our guides to [kidney pain after drinking](/never-hungover/kidney-pain-after-drinking) and [back pain after drinking](/never-hungover/back-pain-after-drinking).

## Left Chest Pain After Drinking

Pain in the left side of the chest deserves its own section because the stakes can be higher.

The most common causes after drinking are harmless ones: heartburn, trapped gas pressing up from the colon bend, and sore chest wall muscles from vomiting or coughing. But alcohol also affects the heart. Heavy drinking, especially a binge, can trigger an irregular heart rhythm, most often atrial fibrillation. Doctors have called this "holiday heart syndrome" since the 1970s because it shows up after weekends and holidays of heavy drinking. It can feel like a racing, fluttering, or pounding heartbeat, sometimes with chest discomfort, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness.

Treat left chest pain as a heart problem until a doctor says otherwise if it comes with any of these: pressure, squeezing, or heaviness in the chest; pain spreading to your arm, jaw, neck, or back; shortness of breath; sweating; nausea; or a heartbeat that's racing or irregular and won't settle. Call 911. Don't drive yourself. For milder symptoms, our guides to [chest pain after drinking](/never-hungover/chest-pain-after-drinking) and [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explain the common causes and the warning signs.

## Left Side Pain the Day After Drinking

Most people notice left-side pain the next morning rather than while they're drinking. That timing fits the common causes. Gas builds up overnight as food and drink ferment, stomach irritation peaks once the alcohol wears off, dehydration is at its worst first thing in the morning, and muscles stiffen after a night of vomiting or sleeping awkwardly.

The pattern that should reassure you: the pain is mild to moderate, it moves around or comes and goes, it improves over the day as you drink water and eat something bland, and it's gone within a day or two.

The pattern that should worry you: the pain is severe, steady, and in one place; it gets worse through the day instead of better; it spreads to your back; you can't keep food or water down; or you have a fever. Pancreatitis, a kidney stone, and diverticulitis all tend to get worse rather than better with time. Pain that's still there or growing after 24 hours deserves a call to a doctor.

## Pain Right After One or Two Drinks

Pain that appears within minutes of having just a small amount of alcohol is a different situation from a next-day ache, and it's worth mentioning to a doctor.

- **Stomach ulcers or gastritis** can cause pain soon after any alcohol hits the stomach.
- **Gallbladder or pancreas problems** can flare with alcohol, especially alongside a fatty meal.
- **Hodgkin lymphoma** is a rare cause, but it's well described in the medical literature: some people with this cancer feel pain in their lymph nodes (often in the neck, armpit, or chest) within minutes of drinking alcohol. It's uncommon, and most people with pain after drinking don't have it, but alcohol-triggered pain in a lump or node, especially with night sweats, weight loss, or fevers, is worth getting checked.

None of these is something to panic about. The point is that pain triggered by small amounts of alcohol isn't a normal hangover symptom, so it's worth a regular appointment rather than waiting.

## How to Tell the Causes Apart: A Side-by-Side Guide

| What it feels like | Where | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sharp, shifting, comes in waves, better after passing gas | Upper left, under ribs; sometimes left chest | Trapped gas | Walk, sip water, avoid carbonation; usually fades in hours |
| Burning or gnawing, with nausea or sour burps | Upper middle or upper left | Gastritis or reflux | Bland food, water, antacid; skip alcohol and ibuprofen |
| Severe, constant, bores into the back, with vomiting | Upper middle or upper left | Pancreatitis | Urgent care or ER the same day |
| Sore spot you can press on, worse with breathing or twisting | Ribs or chest wall | Muscle strain from vomiting | Rest, heat, time |
| Dull, crampy, with no bowel movement for days | Lower left | Constipation | Water, fiber, gentle movement |
| Steady, with fever and change in bowel habits | Lower left | Diverticulitis | See a doctor the same day |
| Sharp, in waves, spreads toward the groin | Left flank or back | Kidney stone | See a doctor; ER if severe |
| Flank pain with fever and burning when you pee | Left flank or back | Kidney infection | See a doctor the same day |
| Pressure in the chest, shortness of breath, racing or uneven heartbeat | Left chest | Heart rhythm or heart problem | Call 911 |

This table is a rough guide, not a diagnosis. Symptoms overlap, and the safest approach is to let severity and warning signs, not location alone, decide what you do next.

## What to Do at Home for Mild Left-Side Pain

If your pain is mild, you don't have any of the warning signs above, and it fits the pattern of gas, an irritated stomach, or constipation, these steps usually help.

1. **Stop drinking alcohol** until the pain is completely gone. More alcohol irritates the stomach further and keeps your gut unsettled.
2. **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water or an electrolyte drink through the day rather than gulping large amounts at once, which can make nausea worse.
3. **Eat small, bland meals.** Toast, crackers, rice, bananas, oatmeal, broth, and eggs are gentle choices. Skip greasy, spicy, and very sugary foods for a day. Fatty meals are a particular problem if your pancreas or gallbladder is involved.
4. **Avoid carbonation** if gas is the issue, including sparkling water and soda.
5. **Move gently.** A short walk helps gas move through your colon. Lying on your left side or drawing your knees toward your chest can also help gas pass.
6. **Use heat** on sore muscles or crampy areas. A warm compress or heating pad on a low setting is fine.
7. **Choose painkillers carefully.** Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate the stomach and make bleeding more likely, especially after drinking, and they're harder on dehydrated kidneys. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but is processed by the liver, so wait until the alcohol has cleared and stick to the label dose. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the safe way to use it.
8. **Try an antacid** for burning upper belly pain. If it helps quickly, reflux or gastritis is the likely cause. Our roundup of the [best antacids after drinking](/never-hungover/best-antacid-after-drinking) compares the options.

Give it a day. If the pain isn't clearly improving within 24 hours, or it's getting worse at any point, stop home care and call a doctor.

## What a Doctor Will Check

If you do get seen, knowing what to expect can make it less daunting. A doctor will usually ask where the pain is, when it started, what it feels like, how much you drank, and whether you've vomited or had a fever. They'll press on your belly to see where it's tender.

Depending on what they suspect, they may order:

- **Blood tests**, including lipase for the pancreas, liver tests, kidney function, and a blood count to check for infection or bleeding
- **A urine test** for blood or infection
- **An ECG** (a quick heart tracing) if you have chest pain or an irregular heartbeat
- **An ultrasound or CT scan** to look at the pancreas, gallbladder, kidneys, or colon
- **A pregnancy test** for women of childbearing age with lower belly pain

Be honest about how much you drank. Doctors aren't there to judge, and the amount genuinely changes how they interpret your symptoms and test results.

## Can You Prevent Left-Side Pain When You Drink?

Most of the common causes respond to the same habits that make any night of drinking easier on your body.

- **Eat a real meal before drinking.** Food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your gut lining and bloodstream. Drinking on an empty stomach is one of the most reliable ways to wake up with an upset stomach. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why.
- **Alternate drinks with water** to limit dehydration, which drives constipation, kidney aches, and stone risk.
- **Go easy on carbonation and sugary mixers** if gas and bloating are your problem.
- **Pace yourself.** Binge drinking is linked to pancreatitis attacks and irregular heart rhythms. Fewer drinks spread over more time is easier on every organ on this list.
- **Skip the greasy late-night meal** if you've noticed upper belly pain after drinking before. Alcohol and a very fatty meal together are a known combination for pancreas and gallbladder flare-ups.
- **Pay attention to patterns.** If you get the same left-side pain every time you drink, that's useful information for a doctor, not something to keep pushing through.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that many people take around drinking. Lab and animal research suggests it may help the body process alcohol and its toxic by-product acetaldehyde, and a small amount of human research has looked at liver markers. The human evidence on hangovers is still limited.

It's important to be clear about what DHM can't do here. There's no good evidence that DHM prevents pancreatitis, gastritis, kidney stones, or heart rhythm problems, and it doesn't make it safe to keep drinking through pain. If you have any of the warning signs in this article, see a doctor and skip both the alcohol and the supplements until you know what's going on.

Because the causes of left-side pain range from trapped gas to pancreatitis, we don't recommend any supplement for it. If the pain is mild and clearly digestive, our guides to [gas after drinking](/never-hungover/gas-after-drinking) and [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) cover home care, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that lower the odds next time. Anything matching the warning signs above needs a doctor, not a product.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my left side hurt after drinking alcohol?**

Most often it's your digestive tract: trapped gas in the bend of the colon under your left ribs, an irritated stomach lining, constipation, or diarrhea. These usually clear up within a day or two. Less often, left-side pain comes from the pancreas, the left kidney, or the heart. Severe, steady pain, pain that spreads to your back, fever, or chest pain with shortness of breath needs medical care.

**Is upper left abdominal pain after drinking pancreatitis?**

Usually not, but it can be. Pancreatitis pain is typically severe and constant, sits in the upper middle or upper left belly, spreads to the back, gets worse after eating, and comes with nausea and vomiting. Gas and gastritis pain tend to be milder, shift around, and improve with time, food, or passing gas. If your pain matches the pancreatitis pattern, go to urgent care or the ER the same day.

**Can drinking alcohol cause pain under the left ribs?**

Yes. The most common reasons are gas trapped where the colon bends under the left ribs, stomach irritation, and sore muscles from vomiting. Pain from the pancreas or an enlarged spleen is less common. If pressing on one spot reproduces the pain and it's worse when you breathe or twist, a muscle cause is likely. Deep, severe, steady pain is more worth getting checked.

**Is left-side pain after drinking my liver?**

Probably not. Your liver sits on the right side, under the right ribs. Left-side pain is more likely to come from your stomach, colon, pancreas, spleen, or left kidney. Pain under the right ribs, especially with yellow skin or eyes or dark urine, is the more relevant sign for the liver.

**What causes lower left abdominal pain after drinking?**

Constipation, gas, diarrhea and cramping, and IBS flare-ups are the usual causes, since the last stretch of the colon sits in the lower left belly. Diverticulitis causes steadier lower left pain, often with fever, and needs a doctor. Women should also consider the left ovary, and any chance of pregnancy with one-sided lower belly pain needs prompt care.

**When should I worry about left side pain after drinking?**

Get emergency care for severe pain that spreads to your back, vomiting you can't stop, bloody or coffee-ground vomit, black stools, chest pain with shortness of breath or sweating, fainting, or a racing or irregular heartbeat. See a doctor the same day for pain with fever, blood in your urine, or pain that keeps getting worse. Book an appointment if it happens every time you drink.

**How long does left side pain from drinking last?**

Pain from gas, mild stomach irritation, or dehydration usually improves within hours and is gone within a day or two. Pain that's still present after 24 hours, or getting worse rather than better, isn't typical of a hangover and should be checked by a doctor.

**Can I take ibuprofen for stomach pain after drinking?**

It's best to avoid it. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate the stomach lining and raise the risk of stomach bleeding, and their labels warn people who have three or more drinks a day. They're also harder on dehydrated kidneys. Acetaminophen is gentler on the stomach but is processed by the liver, so wait until the alcohol has cleared and follow the label. For burning upper belly pain, an antacid is often a better first choice.
